executive_thesis:
In the *Sentencia libri De anima* (c. 1267–1268), Thomas Aquinas provides the psychological and cognitive complement to the epistemological division of the sciences established in *Super Boetium De Trinitate* and the demonstrative logic of the *Expositio libri Posteriorum Analyticorum*. Whereas logic examines how geometric conclusions flow from immediate principles and metaphysics examines the ontological status of continuous quantity, psychology investigates the incarnate acts by which a human soul united to a body abstracts exact mathematical forms without forfeiting contact with spatial extension. Across the three books of the commentary, Aquinas traces an unbroken arc from the critique of Platonic-Pythagorean reifications of points and numbers (Book I, Lecture 11) and the physics of *fluent being* in sensory media (Book II, Lecture 16) to the mature doctrine of *intelligible matter*, *turning to the phantasms*, and the soul as an intellectual instrument analogous to the human hand (Book III, Lectures 8, 12, and 13).

The pivot of this psychological noetics appears in Book III, Lecture 8 (Pirotta nos. 705–716), where Aquinas establishes the structural proportion governing natural and mathematical definitions: *flesh and bones* stand to *the snub* just as the extended *continuum*—which Aquinas identifies as *intelligible matter* (*materia intelligibilis*)—stands to *the straight*. Because quantity inheres immediately in substance prior to *sensible matter* (qualities such as hot, cold, white, and black), the agent intellect can strip away every sensible quality without falsehood while retaining continuous quantity in the intellect as the individuating substrate of geometric figures. Consequently, just as several men share one specific humanity through diverse parcels of *flesh and bones*, numerically distinct congruent triangles share one mathematical quiddity through distinct parts of the *continuum*. Yet because the human intellect directly apprehends only the universal quiddity—like a line extended straight—it knows the singular geometric figure only indirectly by bending back in reflection upon the *phantasm* (*redit super phantasmata*).

Lectures 12 and 13 of Book III complete this architecture by demonstrating why *turning to the phantasms* (*conversio ad phantasmata*) is not merely a genetic stage in learning geometry, as Avicenna supposed, but a permanent structural requirement of every act of contemplation (Pirotta nos. 770–777, 790–791). Because phantasms stand to the intellective soul as sensible objects stand to external sense, the soul never understands without a *phantasm*—even when contemplating *per se* mathematical attributes such as curvature apart from flesh (nos. 780–783). Synthesizing Aristotle's comparison of the soul to the hand as the *organ of organs* (*organum organorum*) and the intellect as the *form of forms* (*species specierum*, nos. 789–791), Aquinas reveals human mathematical reason to be neither an angelic intuition of Platonic Ideas nor an empiricist tally of sensory approximations, but an abstractive insight that beholds universal necessity within the determinate spatial diagram.

conceptual_table.significance: Substance considered solely as subject to continuous quantity after all sensible qualities have been mentally removed; provides the intrinsic substrate included in mathematical definitions and the principle multiplying congruent individuals within a single geometric species.

Corporeal matter subject to sensible qualities (hot, cold, white, black, resistant, soft); essential to natural definitions such as flesh or the snub, but excluded from mathematical definitions such as the curved or the straight.

A particular likeness of a sensible magnitude preserved and formed in the imaginative power; stands to the intellect as the sensible object stands to sense and contains universal intelligibles in potency.

The reflexive return of the intellect upon imaginative representations, required both to know singulars indirectly (like a bent line) and to exercise habitual scientific knowledge in actual contemplation.
Common sensible matter included universally in the natural definition of man, while individual natural substances require determinate ('this') flesh and ('these') bones.
Aristotle's canonical specimen of a natural form-in-matter ('concavity in a nose'), whose very definition inseparably posits determinate sensible matter.
The paradigmatic mathematical attribute whose definition abstracts from all sensible qualities yet necessarily includes the extended continuum as its intelligible matter.

conceptual_table.locus: Lib. I, lect. 11 (no. 172); Lib. III, lect. 8 (no. 713)
conceptual_table.significance: Unbroken quantitative extension divisible without limit and incapable of being composed from unextended points; serves in geometry as the intelligible matter underlying straightness, curvature, and figure.

conceptual_table.latin_term: esse fluens (contra esse fixum et quiescens)
conceptual_table.significance: The successive, motion-dependent mode of existence characteristic of sound and wave propagation in a medium, contrasted with the permanent and resting being (*esse permanens et fixum*) of static qualities and magnitudes.
The classical definition distinguishing the geometric point—situated within the spatial continuum—from the pure arithmetic unit (*unitas intellecta*), which lacks site and position.
Designation of the human hand, which replaces specialized animal appendages by crafting an open-ended array of external instruments; the bodily analogue of the rational soul.

Aristotle's title for the intellect (explicated by Aquinas as the power receptive of all intelligible forms), through which the human soul intentionally becomes 'in a way all things' without possessing any material form restricting its scope.

section_summaries.heading: Book I, Lecture 11 — On Democritus's Account of Motion and How Geometers Imagine a Moving Point Describing a Line
section_summaries.argument_summary:
In Lecture 11 (Pirotta nos. 168–177), Aquinas expounds Aristotle's refutation of Xenocrates's definition of the soul as a 'self-moving number.' Aquinas structures the critique first around the substance of the soul through six dialectical arguments (nos. 169–174), and second around its shared philosophical absurdities and inability to ground psychic operations (nos. 175–177). Because a number resolves into units and a soul existing in a body must have spatial location, Xenocrates's units collapse into 'units having position'—that is, geometric points. Yet as proved in *Physics* VIII, every *per se* self-mover requires a distinction between a moving part and a moved part, which is impossible in an indivisible unit or point (no. 169). Crucially, in the second argument (no. 170), Aquinas invokes the Platonic-geometrical thesis that 'the motion of a point makes a line, while a moved line makes a surface, and a surface a body,' concluding that if the soul were a self-moving point, its motion would generate not biological life, but a mere geometric line.

Aquinas further demonstrates that treating the soul as number violates biological continuity—since adding or subtracting a unit alters the species of a number, whereas divided plants and segmented animals retain the same specific soul (no. 171)—and collapses Xenocrates's mathematical idealism into Democritus's materialism of spherical soul-atoms, since quantified moving units differ only verbally from indivisible corpuscles (nos. 172, 176). Moreover, soul-points either duplicate the body's own intrinsic points—allowing infinitely many indivisibles to occupy a single indivisible place—or are identical with them, rendering every body animate (nos. 173, 175), while points cannot be separated from lines and bodies as the intellective soul is separated (no. 174). Finally, weaving together number and motion fails the scientific criterion of definition (*Posterior Analytics* I), because neither discrete arithmetic nor local motion gives the slightest clue for deducing the soul's proper operations of reasoning, pleasure, and sorrow (no. 177).
key_theses: A geometric point differs from an arithmetic unit solely by adding spatial position (*unitas positionem habens*, nos. 170, 173).
No indivisible unit or point can move itself *per se*, because self-motion requires distinct moving and moved parts (*continuum*, nos. 169, 172).
According to the kinematic mode of speaking used by Platonists and geometers, a moving point generates only a line, not life (no. 170).
Points and lines are ontological boundaries inseparable in real being from surfaces and bodies (no. 174).
A scientific definition must serve as the middle term demonstrating the subject's *per se* attributes and operations, which 'self-moving number' wholly fails to do (no. 177).

section_summaries.heading: Book II, Lecture 16 — On Sound in Act and Potency and Its Fluent Mode of Being in Motion
section_summaries.argument_summary:
In Lecture 16 (Pirotta nos. 438–449), Aquinas introduces Aristotle's treatise on the audible by solving a methodological puzzle: why does *De Anima* investigate the physical generation of sound, whereas earlier it treated color only insofar as color alters the transparent medium and sight? Aquinas replies with a foundational ontological distinction (no. 438): color, odor, flavor, and tangible qualities possess a 'permanent and fixed being in their subject' (*esse permanens et fixum in suo subiecto*), whereas sound is caused by motion and lacks any 'fixed and resting being' (*esse fixum et quiescens*), consisting instead in a dynamic alteration—what scholastic and neo-Thomist natural philosophy terms *fluent being* (*esse fluens*). Consequently, while sound exists in the resonant bell or bronze only in potency, sound in act exists solely in the moved medium and in the sense of hearing (nos. 439–440).

Aquinas then analyzes the triadic mechanics required to actualize sound—a striker, a resistant struck body, and a continuous fluid medium such as air or water (nos. 441–445)—showing that percussion must be swift enough to forestall the dispersion of the air so that the air is struck as a unified mass, like a swiftly struck heap of stones (no. 445). Turning to the secondary generation of sound in echoes (nos. 446–449), Aquinas models acoustic propagation geometrically upon the concentric circular waves (*gyrationes*) formed when a stone is cast into water: near the center of percussion the circles are small and forceful, while at greater radii they expand and weaken until they either vanish or rebound in the contrary direction from a smooth or concave obstacle, analogous to a rebounding sphere (nos. 446–448) and to the specular versus diffuse reflection of solar rays from polished bronze and water versus opaque bodies (no. 449).
key_theses: Unlike color and tangible qualities, which have permanent and fixed being in their subjects, sound has no resting act in the sounding body, but exists in act only in the motion of the medium and in hearing (nos. 438–440).

Actualized sound requires three concurrent principles: a hard, smooth striking body, a resistant struck body, and an undivided continuous medium whose dispersion is forestalled by velocity (nos. 441–445).
Acoustic propagation diffuses radially through air in concentric circular waves whose force diminishes with increasing circumference, parallel to ripples on struck water (nos. 446–447).

Echoes and ambient illumination obey parallel laws of reflection: every wave or ray rebounds, producing a distinct echo from concave enclosures and specular brightness from water or polished bronze, while diffuse reflection from opaque bodies prevents total darkness outside direct sunlight (nos. 448–449).

section_summaries.heading: Book III, Lecture 8 — On the Object of the Intellect: Flesh and Bone vs. the Continuum, the Snub vs. the Straight, and Reflection upon the Phantasm
section_summaries.argument_summary:
Lecture 8 (Pirotta nos. 699–718) is Aquinas's decisive psychological analysis of intellectual habit, mathematical abstraction, and the proper object of the human mind. Beginning with the transition of the possible intellect from pure potency to habitual science (first act) and actual contemplation (second act, nos. 699–703), Aquinas refutes Avicenna's claim that intelligible species are never stored in the possible intellect but must be freshly infused from a separate Agent Intelligence whenever we think (nos. 701–702). Moving to the object of the intellect (nos. 704–709), Aquinas invokes *Metaphysics* VII to distinguish simple immaterial forms—which are identical with their own quiddities—from composite forms in matter, where individuating principles lie outside the specific essence ('Socrates is not his humanity,' no. 705). Crucially, Aquinas extends hylomorphic composition from natural things to mathematics by distinguishing *sensible matter* from *intelligible matter* (nos. 706–707): because continuous quantity inheres immediately in substance prior to sensible qualities (white, black, hot, cold), the intellect can remove sensible qualities while retaining continuous quantity (*continuum*), thereby grounding numerically distinct individuals (such as multiple congruent triangles) within a single mathematical species.

Aquinas then maps cognitive powers onto these ontological levels through a double analogy (nos. 710–716). Just as natural definitions include common *sensible matter* (*flesh and bones* for man, the nose for *the snub*) while abstracting from *this* flesh and *these* bones, mathematical definitions include *intelligible matter* (the *continuum* for *the straight* and the curved) while abstracting from sensible qualities altogether (nos. 713–716). To compare universal essences with singular instances, one and the same intellective soul knows both in distinct modes, illustrated by Aristotle's geometric simile of the bent line (*circumflexa*, nos. 711–712): extended straight, the intellect directly apprehends the universal quiddity; bent back in reflection upon the *phantasms* (*redit super phantasmata*), it indirectly knows the singular. Aquinas concludes by refuting three rival epistemologies at once: Platonic realism, which confuses abstraction in thought with separation in real being (nos. 716); representationalism, since the intelligible species is not *what* is known (*quod*) but *that by which* (*quo*) the extramental quiddity is known (no. 717); and Averroist monopsychism, since numerically distinct intellects share one understood truth through distinct species representing the same real nature (no. 718).
key_theses: Habitual science (*actus primus*) preserves intelligible species in the possible intellect midway between pure potency and actual operation (*actus secundus*), refuting Avicenna's separate Agent Intelligence (nos. 700–702).

Continuous quantity inheres in substance prior to sensible qualities; when sensible qualities are mentally removed, substance under continuous quantity remains in the intellect as *intelligible matter* (nos. 706–707).

*The straight* stands to the *continuum* (*intelligible matter*) just as *the snub* stands to the nose and man stands to *flesh and bones* (*sensible matter*), explaining why multiple triangles exist within a single geometric species (nos. 707, 713, 715).
Like a line extended straight and bent back upon itself, the intellect directly apprehends universal quiddities and indirectly knows singulars by reflecting upon the *phantasms* (nos. 711–712).

Intelligible species are the formal medium *by which* (*quo*) reality is understood, not the primary object *which* (*quod*) is understood, overturning both Platonism and Averroist monopsychism (nos. 716–718).

section_summaries.heading: Book III, Lecture 12 — Why the Soul Never Understands Without a Phantasm and How Mathematical Entities Are Understood in Abstraction
section_summaries.argument_summary:
In Lecture 12 (Pirotta nos. 764–785), Aquinas examines the operation of the intellect in comparison with sensation and appetite. First, he distinguishes physical motion (*actus imperfecti*, a transitive passage from contrary to contrary that destroys the prior quality) from cognitive and volitional operation (*actus perfecti*, the immanent activity of a power already perfected by its species, nos. 764–765). While simple sensation parallels intellectual apprehension, sense quasi-affirms or quasi-denies only particular pleasure and pain through the 'sensitive mean'—likened geometrically to the center of a circle at which all radii from the external senses converge (nos. 766–768, 772)—whereas the intellect strictly affirms and denies universal truth and moves the rational appetite immediately toward universal good (nos. 769–771). From the proportionality *sensibles : sense :: phantasms : intellect*, Aquinas draws Aristotle's cardinal psychological law: 'the soul cannot understand without a phantasm' (no. 771), reinforcing the unity of the judging intellect through the Euclidean alternation of proportions (*permutatio proportionum*, *a* : *b* :: *c* : *d* implies *a* : *c* :: *b* : *d*, no. 775) and showing how deliberation calculates future contingencies in phantasms as though visually present (nos. 776–779).

Having established the universal necessity of *phantasms*, Aquinas confronts the crucial test case of mathematics (nos. 780–785): how can an intellect bound to sensory phantasms understand entities separated from sensible qualities? Invoking the principle that 'there is no falsehood in those who abstract,' Aquinas distinguishes judging two conjoined things *to exist separately* (which would be false) from understanding one *apart from* the other when the latter does not enter its definition (nos. 780–781). Unlike *the snub*, whose definition includes the sensible nose, curvature does not include flesh in its definition; hence the intellect actually understands the curved *without understanding flesh*, contemplating mathematical entities 'as though they were separated, even though they are not separated in reality' (nos. 781–782). Plato's failure to grasp this abstractive precision forced him to posit subsistent Mathematicals and Forms, whereas Aristotle posited the agent intellect (no. 783). Aquinas closes by deferring the metaphysical question of whether our embodied intellect can know wholly immaterial substances (nos. 784–785).
key_theses: Sensing and understanding are not physical alterations (*actus imperfecti*) but immanent operations of a perfected power (*actus perfecti*, nos. 764–765).

Both the common sense and the intellect act as an indivisible discriminating center to which diverse sensory lines or phantasms converge, verified by alternation of proportions (*a : b :: c : d*, nos. 767, 772–775).
Because phantasms stand to the intellective soul as sensibles stand to sense, the human soul never understands without a *phantasm* (no. 771).

Mathematical abstraction involves no falsehood because the intellect understands *the curved* without thinking of flesh—not by judging curvature to subsist apart from sensible bodies, a confusion that led Plato to posit separate Forms in place of the agent intellect (nos. 780–783).

section_summaries.heading: Book III, Lecture 13 — How the Soul Is in a Way All Things, the Hand the Organ of Organs, and the Intellect the Form of Forms
section_summaries.argument_summary:
In Lecture 13 (Pirotta nos. 786–793), Aquinas synthesizes the entire noetics of *De Anima* around two master theses: how the rational soul is intentionally 'all things,' and why human intellection depends intrinsically upon sense and imagination even after scientific habits have been acquired. Recapitulating earlier Greek philosophy (nos. 786–788), Aquinas affirms that the soul is 'in a way all things'—sensible through sense and intelligible through intellect—not materially, as Empedocles imagined ('knowing stone by an internal stone'), but intentionally through immaterial *species* ('a stone is not in the soul, but the species of the stone,' no. 788). Hence the soul corresponds to the human hand (no. 789): just as nature gave humanity the hand as the *organ of organs* (*organum organorum*) in place of fixed claws, horns, or pelts so that humans might fashion universal instruments for every purpose, so the soul is given in place of fixed innate forms as receptive of all sensible and intelligible forms—making the intellect the *form of forms* (*species specierum*).

In the second half of the lecture (nos. 790–793), Aquinas forestalls any Platonist or Avicennian inference that this universal receptivity emancipates human thought from bodily magnitudes. Because neither natural attributes nor mathematical abstractions (*ea quae dicuntur per abstractionem*) subsist outside sensible magnitudes in reality, no human being can either learn science initially or exercise already-acquired science (*utens scientia habita*) without simultaneously forming and inspecting a *phantasm* (no. 790). Against Avicenna's claim that habitual science dispenses with sense and imagination, Aquinas adduces empirical clinical proof: lesion of the bodily organ of imagination impedes the actual use of previously mastered science (no. 791). Nevertheless, intellectual concepts (*primi intellectus*) are never reducible to phantasms: imagination neither combines concepts into true or false judgments (no. 792) nor represents universals as such, for *phantasms* depict singulars and contain universal indivisibles only in potency, not in act (no. 793).
key_theses: The soul is 'in a way all things' not materially like Empedocles's elements, but intentionally by receiving the sensible and intelligible species of things without matter (nos. 786–788).

Just as the hand is the *organ of organs* (*organum organorum*) enabling man to craft every tool, the soul stands in place of all forms, with the intellect functioning as the *form of forms* (*species specierum*) receptive of all intelligibles (no. 789).

Because mathematical and natural intelligibles exist ontologically only within sensible magnitudes, both initial discovery and the actual contemplation of habitual science require forming a *phantasm* (nos. 790–791).
Against Avicenna, bodily lesion of the imaginative organ blocks the exercise of already-acquired science, proving permanent dependence on *turning to the phantasms* (no. 791).

Primary intellectual concepts are not *phantasms*, though never without them: phantasms represent particulars and are universal indivisibles only in potency, while truth and falsehood belong to intellectual judgment alone (nos. 792–793).

section_notes.heading: Book I, Lecture 11 — On Democritus's Account of Motion and How Geometers Imagine a Moving Point Describing a Line
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Aquinas comments here on Aristotle's *De Anima* I.4 (408b32–409b18), continuing the critique of kinetic theories of the soul begun at I.3 (406b15–25, where Democritus's spherical fire-atoms and Plato's *Timaeus* circles were first paired). Xenocrates, scholarch of the Old Academy after Speusippus, sought to synthesize Platonic mathematical metaphysics with kinetic psychology by defining the soul as 'number moving itself' (ἀριθμὸς κινῶν ἑαυτόν). Following Aristotle's cross-references to *Physics* VI (an indivisible cannot move *per se*, nor compose a continuum) and *Physics* VIII (every self-mover divides into an unmoved or moving part and a moved part), Aquinas exposes a fatal category mistake: once arithmetic units are localized inside an animate body, they acquire spatial position (*positio* / θέσις) and become indistinguishable either from geometric points or from Democritus's corpuscular atoms, rendering them incapable of either self-motion or biological formal causality.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Paragraph 170 directly engages the foundational tension in Greek geometry between static essential definitions and genetic or kinematic descriptions. In Euclid's *Elements*, Book I, Definitions 1–4 define the point ('that which has no part'), line ('breadthless length'), extremities of a line, and straight line purely statically by boundaries and dimensional privation, without invoking motion; yet Postulates 1–3 ('to draw a straight line from any point to any point,' 'to produce a finite straight line continuously,' 'to describe a circle with any center and distance') and Book XI's solid revolutions (spheres, cones, and cylinders generated by rotating semicircles, triangles, and rectangles) rely on kinematic construction. Proclus (*In Euclidem*, p. 97 and p. 185, citing Geminus) preserves the Academic characterization of the line as the 'flux of a point' (ῥύσις τοῦ σημείου) and the straight line as an 'even and undeviating flux.' Aquinas's exposition clarifies why Euclid excluded motion from Book I's essential definitions of point and line while retaining constructive postulates: motion belongs to the geometer's imaginative generation of figures, whereas ontological priority in the continuum proceeds from solid body down to bounding surface, line, and point (no. 174).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In *De Noetica Geometriae*, Chapter IV, § 2 (with footnotes 8 and 9 citing *In I De Anima*, lect. 11, Pirotta no. 170 alongside *In De Caelo* I, lect. 2, no. 9 and *In Physicorum* IV, lect. 18, no. 4), Peter Hoenen S.J. highlights Aquinas's precise epistemological diagnosis: whereas Aristotle's text at 409a4 simply says 'they say' (φασι) that a moved point makes a line—prompting Trendelenburg to wonder whether the Pythagoreans or all geometers were meant—Aquinas identifies the ontological thesis as Platonist here (no. 170) while elsewhere attributing the idiom to 'geometers imagining (*imaginantes*) that a moved point makes a line.' Hoenen uses this distinction to resolve modern objections (such as Bertrand Russell's and Hermann von Helmholtz's critiques of superposition and kinematic geometry): geometry does not treat physical efficient causality or temporal velocity, which belong to physics, but legitimately employs imagined continuous motion as a genetic *description* (not a strict definition) grounded in the homogeneity of spatial extension as *intelligible matter* and principle of individuation, from which both passive rigid-body mobility and constant direction necessarily flow.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's distinction between the arithmetic unit lacking position, the geometric point as a 'unit having position' (*unitas positionem habens*), and the kinematic imagination of a point tracing a line illuminates the core architectural duality of GEOMETOR. Within ``geometor.model``, points are not floating-point pixels or Democritean corpuscles of small breadth, but exact algebraic indivisibles endowed with symbolic coordinates—literally exact units possessing position within an algebraic field over the rationals and quadratic surds. Meanwhile, when ``geometor.explorer`` animates a compass sweep or straightedge extension across the SVG canvas, it enacts precisely the geometer's kinematic imagination described in Pirotta no. 170: the visual sweep does not *constitute* the algebraic essence of the line or circle, which exists timelessly in polynomial incidence relations, yet it renders the genetic dependency graph of the construction transparent to human intuition.

section_notes.heading: Book II, Lecture 16 — On Sound in Act and Potency and Its Fluent Mode of Being in Motion
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Commenting on Aristotle's *De Anima* II.8 (419b4–420a19), Aquinas situates acoustics within Aristotle's hierarchy of the external senses: sight perceives through a purely spiritual or intentional immutation of the pellucid medium, whereas hearing perceives through local motion propagated across air or water. Aquinas's methodological prologue (no. 438) coordinates the entire Aristotelian *libri naturales*—cross-referencing *De Sensu et Sensato* for color, flavor, and odor, *De Generatione et Corruptione* for tangible contraries, and *Meteorologica*—to explain why sound alone must be analyzed *in fieri* within *De Anima* itself: because sound possesses no static accident residing in the bronze bell, its formal actuality is inseparable from the kinetic propagation of percussion through an undivided medium.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas's exposition of acoustic propagation and reverberation (nos. 446–449) deploys explicitly Euclidean geometric models of radial symmetry and catoptric reflection. First, the diffusion of compressed air from the locus of percussion is modeled as a family of concentric circular waves (*gyrationes*) expanding outward from a center (Euclid, *Elements* I, Def. 15), where wave intensity varies inversely with radial distance. Second, Aquinas pairs acoustic echoes from smooth or concave vessels with the optical reflection of light rays from water and polished bronze (*aes*, rendering Aristotle's χαλκός at 419b31), invoking the geometric law of reflection systematized in the Euclidean *Catoptrics*—where incident and reflected rays make equal angles with a smooth surface, while concave surfaces converge and multiply reflected impulses and rough opaque surfaces scatter light diffusely so as to prevent total shadow outside direct solar rays.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In the metaphysical Appendix to *De Noetica Geometriae* ('Additions,' nos. 1–2, citing *In II De Anima*, lect. 16 alongside *In IV Physicorum*, lect. 17 and *De Potentia*, q. 7, a. 2, ad 9), Hoenen elevates Aquinas's contrast between permanent qualities and sound lacking 'a fixed and resting *esse* in the subject' (no. 438) into a general theory of existential modes of being. Motion strictly speaking possesses a continuous *fluent being* (*esse fluens*) whose successive duration and variable velocity exhibit quantitative and structural proper attributes analogous—yet irreducibly heterogeneous—to permanent spatial extension. Tracing a line from Aquinas and Nicole Oresme's medieval 'configurations of qualities across temporal duration' to modern wave mechanics and quantum photons, Hoenen shows how periodic, oscillatory variations in *fluent being* explain acoustic pitch and optical color without collapsing four-dimensional spacetime calculations into a univocal geometric continuum.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's contrast between permanent, resting form (*esse permanens et fixum*) and *fluent being* (*esse fluens*) propagating in concentric circular waves directly mirrors the interplay between static structural invariants and dynamic wave-like propagation in GEOMETOR constructions. In ``geometor.model``, each compass construction radiates from a struck center across a chosen radial distance, generating new intersection loci step by step along a directed acyclic graph whose expanding rings echo the concentric *gyrationes* of Lecture 16. While the completed symbolic model retains permanent algebraic being—every golden ratio proportion and harmonic cross-ratio discovered by ``geometor.divine`` holds timelessly—the constructive sequence animated in ``geometor.explorer`` unfolds in *fluent being*, allowing the inquirer to witness how local percussions of point and radius reverberate across the entire geometric field.

section_notes.heading: Book III, Lecture 8 — On the Object of the Intellect: Flesh and Bone vs. the Continuum, the Snub vs. the Straight, and Reflection upon the Phantasm
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Expounding the notoriously terse and contested text of *De Anima* III.4 (429b5–22), Aquinas weaves together *Metaphysics* VII (Z.6 and Z.10–11 on essence, individual composites, and intelligible matter) with *De Anima* III to solve how a single immaterial faculty relates to hylomorphic things. Aristotle contrasts concrete magnitudes and natural substances ('water' vs. 'to be for water,' 'flesh' vs. 'to be for flesh') with mathematical abstractions ('the straight' vs. 'to be for the straight,' provisionally illustrated by the Academic formula of duality), comparing *the straight* with *the snub* (τὸ σιμόν) because both involve a substrate—continuous extension (τὸ συνεχές) in the former, sensible nose in the latter. Against Avicenna's extrinsic emanationism (nos. 701–702), Plato's separated Forms and Mathematicals (nos. 704, 716), and Averroes's single separate possible intellect (no. 718), Aquinas defends an intrinsic human intellect that preserves habitual species, abstracts universal quiddities from individuation, and bends back (*circumflexa*, 429b16) upon sensory powers to know singulars.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Lecture 8 supplies the ontological warrant for two pillars of Euclid's *Elements*: the multiplicity of congruent figures (Book I, Prop. 4 and Common Notion 4) and the definition of straightness within continuous magnitude (Book I, Def. 4). If mathematical forms were wholly separated from matter like Platonic Ideas, there could exist only one unique Triangle-Itself and one unique Circle-Itself, making Euclidean constructions—such as erecting an equilateral triangle upon a given segment by intersecting *two* distinct circles in Book I, Prop. 1, or comparing *two* distinct triangles *ABC* and *DEF* in Prop. 4—metaphysically impossible. Aquinas's demonstration that continuous quantity remains in the intellect as *intelligible matter* (nos. 706–707) explains how numerically distinct triangles share an identical specific essence while differing solely by site within the *continuum*, and how *the straight* (no. 713) is essentially an affection of continuous extension.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In *De Noetica Geometriae*, Chapter II, § 7 (Note 1) and Chapter IV, §§ 3–4, Hoenen identifies *De Anima* III, Lecture 8 (together with *Summa Theologiae* I, q. 85, a. 1, ad 2 and *Super Boetium De Trinitate*, q. 5, a. 3) as the keystone solving both fundamental problems of geometric epistemology: *necessity* and *exactitude*. Hoenen emphasizes that in formal abstraction 'matter' signifies what is opaque to intellective intuition (sensible qualities), whereas *intelligible matter* (ὕλη νοητή)—the extended *continuum* retained by formal abstraction—is thoroughly transparent to the human mind as pure potency for geometric figures. Moreover, Hoenen demonstrates that intuiting this homogeneous *continuum* purely as the principle of individuation (differentiating figures by site and number alone, Pirotta nos. 705–707) justifies Euclidean congruence without assuming physically rigid bodies (refuting Poincaré) and establishes both the *quid est* and mathematical existence (*an est*) of exact *straight* lines of constant direction and uniform planes.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's double doctrine in Lecture 8—*intelligible matter* individuating geometric species and the bent-line reflection (*redit super phantasmata*) linking universal quiddity to singular instance—provides the exact philosophical blueprint for the coupling of ``geometor.model`` and ``geometor.explorer``. In ``geometor.model``, a geometric element is defined free of all *sensible matter* (stroke width, pixel rasterization, or pigment), yet never as a Platonic form divorced from *intelligible matter*: distinct lines and circles are individuated within the symbolic *continuum* by their exact algebraic coordinates and polynomial equations, permitting arbitrarily many congruent circles and Golden Sections under one universal ratio. Conversely, whenever the researcher inspects a specific constructed locus on the ``geometor.explorer`` canvas and traces it back to its exact SymPy expression, the workflow performs Aquinas's cognitive reflection—extending straight to grasp the universal algebraic relation and bending back upon the determinate visual *phantasm* to verify its singular instantiation.

section_notes.heading: Book III, Lecture 12 — Why the Soul Never Understands Without a Phantasm and How Mathematical Entities Are Understood in Abstraction
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Aquinas expounds *De Anima* III.7 (431a1–b19), a dense dossier of Aristotelian insights uniting cognitive psychology, theory of action, and philosophy of mathematics. Beginning from the crucial distinction at 431a4–7 between physical *kinesis* (incomplete act of the imperfect) and cognitive *energeia* or *operatio* (complete act of the perfected power, nos. 764–765), Aquinas traces Aristotle's analogy between sensory discrimination and intellectual judgment (431a8–b2), culminating in the celebrated dictum at 431a16–17: διὸ οὐδέποτε νοεῖ ἄνευ φαντάσματος ἡ ψυχή ('wherefore the soul never understands without a phantasm,' no. 771). Aquinas then unpacks 431b12–19 on τὰ ἐν ἀφαιρέσει λεγόμενα ('things spoken of in abstraction,' nos. 780–783), showing how Aristotle replaces Platonic *chorismos* (ontological separation) with selective attention of the agent intellect, which contemplates *the curved* without flesh while never falsely judging curvature to subsist apart from bodies.
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Two explicit mathematical structures govern Aquinas's commentary in Lecture 12. First, to explain how a single indivisible cognitive power discriminates heterogeneous or contrary qualities without splitting into separate subjects, Aquinas twice invokes the Euclidean circle (Book I, Def. 15): both the common sense and the judging intellect stand as a single unextended center at which multiple radial lines from the external senses and phantasms terminate simultaneously (nos. 767, 772). Second, in paragraph 775, Aquinas formalizes Aristotle's lettered proportion at 431a25–29 using Book V, Proposition 16 of Euclid's *Elements* (*permutatio proportionum* or *alternando*): if sensible *a* (white) stands to sensible *b* (black) as phantasm *c* stands to phantasm *d*, then by alternation *a* stands to *c* as *b* stands to *d*, proving rigorously that one unified intellect judges *c* and *d* just as one unified sense judges *a* and *b*. Finally, nos. 780–782 ground the legitimacy of Euclidean geometry's idealized curves and surfaces: abstracting *the curved* from sensible flesh involves no mendacity because sensible qualities fall outside curvature's formal ratio.
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In *De Noetica Geometriae*, Chapter I, § 2 (explicitly citing *De Anima* III.7, 431a14–b2 and Aquinas, Lecture 12, Pirotta nos. 770–772 and 777 alongside *Posterior Analytics* I.12, 77b30) and Chapter III, Hoenen demonstrates that mathematical abstraction is an *intuition conjoined with abstraction* occurring *within* the phantasm: ταῦτα δ' ἐστὶν οἷον ὁρᾶν τῇ νοήσει ('these mathematicals are, as it were, seen by intellection'). Confronting the sensory 'threshold of exactitude' (*limen exactitudinis*)—the fact that neither eye nor imagination can distinguish a true breadthless line or exact concurrency of three medians from a slight deviation—Hoenen shows from Lecture 12 that the intellect does not merely copy blurry phantasms (Mill's empiricism) nor fabricate axioms *a priori* apart from experience (modern formalism). Instead, inspecting the concrete *phantasm*, the agent intellect abstracts formal spatial relations apart from sensible defects (nos. 780–783) and intuits exact, necessary nexus directly in the imagined configuration.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Lecture 12 directly addresses the central epistemological paradox of computational geometry: why visual rendering remains indispensable even when symbolic algebra possesses infinite exactitude. Human perception and screen displays are bounded by Hoenen's *limen exactitudinis*—finite SVG stroke widths and floating-point viewport coordinates in ``geometor.explorer`` are sensible approximations—yet 'the soul cannot understand without a phantasm' (no. 771). In GEOMETOR, ``geometor.explorer`` supplies the luminous, structured *phantasm* in which the geometer visually deliberates and spots candidate collinearities, concurrencies, and golden sections 'as though actually seeing them' (no. 777), while ``geometor.model`` performs the precise non-mendacious abstraction of nos. 780–783: stripping away every pixel approximation to verify in pure symbolic algebra whether curvature, straightness, and harmonic proportion hold *per se*.

section_notes.heading: Book III, Lecture 13 — How the Soul Is in a Way All Things, the Hand the Organ of Organs, and the Intellect the Form of Forms
section_notes.aristotelian_foundations: Commenting on *De Anima* III.8 (431b20–432a14), Aquinas brings Aristotle's treatise on the cognitive powers to its grand architectural synthesis. Aristotle recapitulates his critique of Pre-Socratic materialism from Book I (such as Empedocles's physical isomorphism, 'by earth we see earth,' 404b13), reinterpreting the ancient insight through hylomorphic intentionality: ἡ ψυχὴ τὰ ὄντα πώς ἐστι πάντα ('the soul is in a way all beings,' 431b21) because sense receives sensible forms without matter and intellect receives intelligible forms. At 432a1–3 Aristotle crowns this doctrine with the celebrated proportion: ὥστε ἡ ψυχὴ ὥσπερ ἡ χείρ ἐστιν· καὶ γὰρ ἡ χεὶρ ὄργανόν ἐστιν ὀργάνων, καὶ ὁ νοῦς εἶδος εἰδῶν ('so that the soul is like the hand; for the hand is the organ of organs, and the intellect is the form of forms,' no. 789), before insisting at 432a3–14 that because no intelligible exists apart from sensible magnitudes, anyone contemplating in act must simultaneously behold a *phantasm* (ἅμα φάντασμά τι θεωρεῖν, nos. 790–793).
section_notes.euclidean_counterparts: Aquinas's insistence in nos. 790–791 that even a master possessing habitual geometry cannot contemplate in act without forming a singular *phantasm* illuminates the classical formal structure of every proposition in Euclid's *Elements* (analyzed by Proclus into *protasis*, *ekthesis*, *diorismos*, *kataskeue*, *apodeixis*, and *symperasma*). Euclid never proves a universal *protasis* ('On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle,' or 'In right-angled triangles the square on the hypotenuse equals the squares on the sides') through imageless verbal syllogisms alone; instead, he immediately performs an *ekthesis* ('Let *AB* be the given finite straight line') and *kataskeue* (auxiliary circles and segments), instantiating a singular sensible-imaginative diagram. As Aquinas explains in no. 793, the Euclidean diagram (*phantasma*) is particular in representation yet contains the universal geometric truth in potency, while the compass and straightedge themselves exemplify manual instruments crafted by the hand as *organ of organs* (no. 789).
section_notes.hoenen_noetics: In *De Noetica Geometriae*, Chapter I, § 2 (citing *De Anima* III.8, 432a5–9 and Aquinas, Lecture 13, Pirotta no. 791) and Chapter V (on symbolic logic and *logica utens*), Hoenen deploys Aquinas's anti-Avicennian argument to critique modern mathematical logicism and Hilbertian pure formalism. Just as Avicenna imagined that once the intellect has acquired scientific habits it can operate purely among abstract intentions without returning to sensory imagination—a thesis refuted by Aquinas both ontologically and clinically (no. 791)—radical formalists suppose that once axioms are encoded in 'transcendent terms' (symbolic letters *a*, *b*, *c*), geometry dispenses with spatial intuition altogether. Hoenen acknowledges (quoting Hadamard on Hilbert) the immense utility of stable symbolic formulas as intellectual instruments, yet proves from Pirotta no. 791 that symbols retain real geometric meaning and truth (which belongs solely to intellectual composition and division, no. 792) only insofar as the mind vitalizes them through ongoing *turning to the phantasms*.
section_notes.geometor_significance: Aquinas's analogy of the hand as the *organ of organs* (*organum organorum*) and the intellect as the *form of forms* (*species specierum*, no. 789), paired with the permanent necessity of the *phantasm* in habitual contemplation (nos. 790–791), articulates the deepest philosophical identity of the GEOMETOR ecosystem. Symbolic computation in ``geometor.model``, automated proportional discovery in ``geometor.divine``, propositional DAG reconstruction in ``geometor.elements``, and interactive visualization in ``geometor.explorer`` are intellectual extensions of the *organ of organs*—universal cognitive instruments crafted by human reason in place of fixed biological instincts. Crucially, GEOMETOR refuses the Avicennian or formalist severance of algebra from vision: ``geometor.model`` never replaces the visual *phantasm* of ``geometor.explorer``, nor is geometric truth reduced to the mere image on the canvas (no. 793); rather, exact symbolic reason and luminous spatial imagination operate in continuous synergy whenever the geometer contemplates in act.
